title: Pondweed & The Bubble Test
welcome_lead: Today you'll set up the classic pondweed experiment and learn how scientists count variables.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Here's the classic set-up.

1. Put a piece of pondweed (Elodea) cut-end up in a beaker of water.

2. Add a pinch of sodium hydrogencarbonate to keep CO₂ topped up.

3. Place a lamp at a measured distance.

4. Wait 1 minute for the plant to settle, then count bubbles of oxygen rising from the cut stem for 1 minute.

5. Repeat at different lamp distances — closer = brighter.

Every experiment has three kinds of variable.

Independent — what YOU change. Here: distance from the lamp.

Dependent — what you MEASURE. Here: bubbles per minute.

Control variables — what stays the SAME so the test is fair: temperature, CO₂ level, type of pondweed, water volume, same lamp.

If you forget a control variable, you can't tell what really caused the change.

The bubbles are oxygen — a product of photosynthesis.

More bubbles per minute → faster photosynthesis. Fewer bubbles → slower.

For better accuracy, you can collect the gas in an inverted measuring cylinder and measure volume per minute instead — that fixes the problem of bubbles being different sizes.

mcqs.q: In the pondweed practical, what is the INDEPENDENT variable?
options: Number of bubbles per minute
Distance of the lamp
Temperature of the water
Type of pondweed

mcqs.q: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water?
options: To kill bacteria
To provide a steady supply of CO₂
To make water more acidic
To absorb oxygen
Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
Plants only respire at night and only photosynthesise during the day; the processes never overlap.
Plants only photosynthesise and do not respire; respiration is for animals only.
Yes — plants respire all the time to release energy; they also photosynthesise when there is light.

mcqs.q: Where do plants get most of their biomass from?
options: Plants gain most of their mass directly from sunlight, which has weight.
Plants only respire at night and only photosynthesise during the day; the processes never overlap.
Plants get most of their mass from the soil through their roots.
From carbon dioxide in the air — the carbon in plant tissue comes mostly from CO2 fixed during photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Why is ATP described as an 'energy currency' rather than energy storage?
options: Plants only respire at night and only photosynthesise during the day; the processes never overlap.
ATP is permanent and accumulates with age in cells.
ATP is constantly made and broken down — it transfers energy between reactions rather than storing large amounts for later.
Cells store large amounts of ATP for emergency use.

mcqs.q: You count 45 oxygen bubbles in 3 minutes. What is the rate in bubbles per minute?
A student counts oxygen bubbles from pondweed at different lamp distances. At 10 cm there are 40 bubbles/min and at 20 cm there are 10 bubbles/min. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis.
Temperature is the limiting factor here.
The pondweed respires faster in brighter light.
Distance has no effect on photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: Why should the temperature of the water be kept constant during the pondweed light experiment?
options: So it is a fair test and only light intensity varies
To make the pondweed respire faster
To kill bacteria in the water
Because temperature is the variable being measured

mcqs.q: A student doubles the light intensity and the bubble rate stops increasing. Which factor is most likely now limiting the rate?
options: Carbon dioxide concentration or temperature
Light intensity
The number of bubbles counted
The size of the test tube

mcqs.q: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water around the pondweed?
options: To provide a steady supply of carbon dioxide
To increase the light intensity
To absorb the oxygen produced
To raise the temperature of the water
